messages.subject: Re: Mark-recapture Distance sampling with point transects
messages.subject_clean: Mark-recapture Distance sampling with point transects
messages.body_plain:
James Martin wrote:
> > Hello List,
> >
> > I wanted to double check to see if MRDS with point transects was still not an option with the latest version. If not, I was wondering when this was going to be an option?
> >
It is currently not an option but it is something I've been considering
to add in this next year.  You can use something like MARK to estimate
a combined g(0) and then use that with point transect distances in
Distance but that only works if you have no covariates for the
mark-recapture data.
> >
> > A related aside: I notice with the Golftees example that the distances for each observer are the same. Is this mandatory? or just an artifact of that particular dataset?
> >
Not an artifact.  There is currently no code in Distance that handles
measurement error so all measurements of distance and covariates are
assumed to be without error which by definition means they must be the
same when seen for both observers.

--jeff

he

messages.subject: Re: combining distance and removal data in Program Distance
messages.subject_clean: combining distance and removal data in Program Distance
messages.body_plain:
Vicki-

Your assessment is correct. There is no facility for this in Distance.
In some ways this is similar to the last posting but would
be handled differently in the analysis and would most likely involve
more than 2 occasions.  I'm not a big fan of the approach you are using
because it ignores movement which could lead to substantial positive
bias.  But that said, you can proceed by using a removal model
in MARK to estimate g(0) and then enter that with its std error into
Distance.  Just as with the last post, this works as long as there are
no additional covariates like species, habitat etc that affect g(0).  If
you do have that situation then you would need to stratify your distance
data
and do separate analysis with separate g(0) values.

regards --jeff

messages.subject: Re: Mangrove birds-internal errors-ignore?
messages.body_plain:
Azlan:

Hard to tell exactly what those errors mean without looking more deeply
at the Distance project, but anytime Distance produces an error or
warning message it is something to think about.  You should ponder
whether what Distance is having trouble doing, is something you really
ought to have it do.

According to the Appendix of the Distance Users Guide, both of the
messages you mention (102 and 76) arise from the multiple covariate
(MCDS) engine rather than the CDS engine.  My suspicion is that there
are some combinations of the covariates (are you using species as a
covariate?) for which you have few data and there are difficulties in
fitting a detection function.  I would doubt that the mechanical
remedies that you tried will be of much value.

stion is=20

really basic or if it's obvious that I'm doing something wrong.

trapping webs.  The webs are composed of 12 60-m transects with 8 rings o=
f=20
traps.  There are 4 additional traps at the center for a total of 100 tra=
ps per=20
web.  Data were the number of new captures over the 4-night trapping=20
period, entered individually.  I specified intervals using the midpoints =
between=20
the rings to define the bins.=20=20

I've gotten what seem to be reasonable density estimates using the half-

normal and negative exponential models, but the uniform key does not seem=
 to=20
be working for any of my webs.  It gives me a density estimate, but the=20=

number of parameters is 0, as is the CV.  Both confidence limits equal th=
e=20

density estimate.  I set up the uniform models the same way as the half-
normal and negative exponenial, so I'm not sure what I'm doing wrong.

Any advice would be greatly appreicated.

Thanks in advance,

Carolyn Gillen

Cooperative Wildlife Research Laboratory
Southern Illinois University

messages.subject: Re: Problem running Uniform key models for trapping webs
messages.subject_clean: Problem running Uniform key models for trapping webs
messages.body_plain:
Carolyn:

Here is my suspicion about your analysis.  When fitting the uniform key with any
sort of adjustments to trapping web data, there exists the possibility that no
adjustment terms are necessary to fit your data.  That results in a fitted
model that fits a horizontal detection function (no diminution in detectability
as you move out on the rings of your web).  In this situation, p is estimated to
be 1 for all rings; there are no parameters being estimated because p=1 at the
centre of the the web (by assumption).  Without parameters being estimated,
there is no uncertainty associated with the density or abundance estimates.

This only arises for the uniform key, because the half normal (negative
exponential is not a good key function to use, and you should not really
consider its use) and hazard rate key functions have a decreasing detection
function as a characteristic of the key function.  The decrease in
detectability when using the uniform as the key function comes as a result of
the adjustment terms (which are used/not used as a result of AIC model
selection by Distance default).

The emphasis is not really on the fitting or behaviour of the detection function
fitting, but rather your data.  It is not unlikely with trapping web data that
you have edge effects with large numbers of captures in our outer ring(s).  As
a result, the fitting algorithm believes that detectability does not drop with
distance from web centre, but actually might be increasing with distance from
centre.  However, Distance has constraints that will not allow detection
functions to increase with distance, so the compromise seen with the uniform
key function is to make the detection function flat.  The estimate of abundance
is then equal to the number of captures, because detectability is estimated to
be perfect.  This is probably the fault of the edge effects which are a symptom
of trapping webs.

messages.body_plain:
Carolyn, (list)

I agree with Eric re uniform+no adjustments, likely caused by edge effects.

If you marked trapped animals, and recorded recaptures, you may want to
use the Spatially Explicit Capture Recapture framework for analysis
instead.  You can analyze the data using the software Density
http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/
(references are also on that web site) or WinBUGS (code and book
reference at
http://www.mbr-pwrc.usgs.gov/pubanalysis/roylebook/
).  Takes a bit of work to properly understand this alternative
framework, however.

Hope this helps,

  - Len

messages.subject: Left truncation in MRDS
messages.body_plain:
Hello

I am analysing a dataset that shows reduced sighting frequency close
to the trackline, probably because of an obscured view. I am using
left truncation in conventional models, but left truncation is not
supported in MRDS models.

So, I was considering left-truncating the data outside of DISTANCE,
then subtracting the left truncation distance from all the remaining
distances, then running MRDS models without left truncation. Would
this produce valid results or am I missing something important here?

Thanks,

Daniel Pike.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

I assume that, because you're using MRDS, you have double-observer data.
  In this case, there's no downside I can think of to the strategy you
suggest.  If you have single observer data, then you would be assuming
that detection probability at the left truncation distance is 1.0, but
this is reasonable in many cases anyway.

Cheers, - Len

messages.subject: Re: Bootstrap variance with g(0)
messages.body_plain:
Yes.  There is no way to include generically a non-parametric bootstrap
of g(0).  It could be included parametrically but there really is no
logic or reason to do so.  Instead, you can take the std deviation of
your  bootrstrap abundances and add in the variance for g(0).

var(D*g(0))= (D*g(0))^2*[cv^2(D) +cv^2(g(0))]

where cv^2(D) = (bootstrap std dev of D)^2/D^2

--jeff

messages.subject: Re: Estimating density per point?
messages.body_plain:
Eva:

My suspicion is that this will be very difficult.  Unless you have
dozens of detections of each of your species at each of your points, you
will need to make some compromises.  You may need to use global (pooled)
detection functions across points (or across species) to do what you
wish.  However using these pooled detection functions in conjunction
with your point-specific counts will introduce dependencies between your
point-specific estimates.  As such, you will not be able to make simple
comparisons of density between points because they are dependent because
of the shared detection function.

You might look at a similar question and answer by searching the
archives of the Distance-Sampling list (message 1417-1471 from 11 August
of this year.
